title: Area
subject: Maths-2
description: Areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, rhombuses and trapeziums by dissection, equal-area transformations from the Śulba-Sūtras, shortest paths by reflection, and unit conversions for real-life areas.

questions.question: A rectangle has sidelengths 7 cm and 4 cm. How many non-overlapping unit squares (side 1 cm) can be packed into it?
questions.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 7 × 4 = 28, so 28 unit squares fit. 24 is the 8 × 3 rectangle, 22 is the perimeter and 11 is 7 + 4.

questions.question: Two rangoli rectangles are coloured evenly: one is 7 cm × 4 cm and the other is 8 cm × 3 cm. Which needs more rangoli powder?
options: The 8 cm × 3 cm one, since 24 > 28
The 7 cm × 4 cm one, since 28 > 24
Both need the same, as 11 = 11
The 8 cm × 3 cm one, as it is longer
questions.explanation: Powder needed depends on area. 7 × 4 = 28 cm² is more than 8 × 3 = 24 cm². Being longer (8 cm) does not make the second rectangle bigger in area.

questions.question: The area of a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle can be written either as 28 sq. cm or as 28 cm².
questions.explanation: Both notations mean the same thing: 28 unit squares of side 1 cm. 'sq. cm' and 'cm²' are two ways of writing square centimetres.

questions.question: A rectangle has area 35 in² and one side of length 7 in. What is the length of the other side?
options: 6 in
4 in
5 in
28 in
questions.explanation: Since area = length × width, the missing side = 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in. Subtracting (35 − 7 = 28) is a common slip; area is a product, not a sum.

questions.question: A square plot of area 50 m² is divided into three rectangular parts. Two of them have areas 29 m² and 11 m². What is the area of the third part?
options: 21 m²
39 m²
12 m²
10 m²
questions.explanation: The parts together make up the whole: 50 − 29 − 11 = 10 m². 21 and 39 come from subtracting only one of the two given parts.

questions.question: A square is divided into regions 1, 2 and 3. If the sidelength of the square is doubled (keeping the same picture), what happens to the area of each region?
options: Each becomes 4 times as large
Each becomes 3 times as large
Each becomes 8 times as large
Each becomes 2 times as large
questions.explanation: Doubling the side doubles both the length and the width of every part of the figure, so every area is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4 — region 1, 2 and 3 alike.

questions.question: There are only a finite number of ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area.
questions.explanation: The chapter shows that by compressing one edge and expanding another by the same amount you can alter any division endlessly — there are infinitely many ways.

questions.question: A rectangle contains 28 unit squares of side 1 cm. In which unit is its area written?
options: m²
cm²
cm
cm³
questions.explanation: Area is counted in unit squares, so the unit is square centimetres, cm². Plain cm measures length; cm³ measures volume; m² would be far too large a unit here.

questions.question: Select the statements that correctly describe how area is measured.
options: Area counts the non-overlapping unit squares that fill a region
A unit square may be split into fractions when a region needs it
A longer boundary always means a region has a larger area
The area of a rectangle is twice its length plus its width
questions.explanation: Area is the number of unit squares (possibly fractional) whose area equals the region's. Boundary length (perimeter) is NOT a measure of area, and 2(l + w) is the perimeter, not the area.

questions.question: Why can't the perimeter of a region be used as a measure of its area?
options: Perimeter is always numerically larger than the area
Perimeter can only be found for rectangles and squares
Regions with the same perimeter can have different areas
Perimeter is measured in cm², which cannot count squares
questions.explanation: The chapter's reason: two regions can have the same perimeter but different areas (and vice versa), so knowing the perimeter tells you nothing definite about the area.

questions.question: Rectangle P is 10 cm × 1 cm and rectangle Q is 4 cm × 4 cm. Which statement is correct?
options: Q has the greater perimeter but the smaller area
P and Q have equal perimeters but different areas
P has the greater perimeter and the greater area
P has the greater perimeter but the smaller area
questions.explanation: P: perimeter 2(10 + 1) = 22 cm, area 10 cm². Q: perimeter 16 cm, area 16 cm². So the larger perimeter (P) goes with the smaller area.

questions.question: If two regions have equal perimeters, they must also have equal areas.
questions.explanation: No — a 10 × 1 rectangle and a 6 × 5 rectangle both have perimeter 22, but areas 10 and 30. Equal perimeter does not force equal area.

questions.question: Four rectangles all have perimeter 20 cm. Which one has the greatest area?
options: 5 cm × 5 cm
9 cm × 1 cm
6 cm × 4 cm
8 cm × 2 cm
questions.explanation: Areas are 25, 24, 16 and 9 cm². Same perimeter, very different areas — and the most 'square-like' rectangle has the most area.

questions.question: Which pair of rectangles shows Perimeter(R1) > Perimeter(R2) but Area(R1) < Area(R2)?
options: R1: 5 cm × 5 cm, R2: 4 cm × 4 cm
R1: 9 cm × 1 cm, R2: 4 cm × 3 cm
R1: 4 cm × 3 cm, R2: 9 cm × 1 cm
R1: 6 cm × 2 cm, R2: 4 cm × 3 cm
questions.explanation: 9 × 1: perimeter 20, area 9. 4 × 3: perimeter 14, area 12. So R1 has the bigger perimeter and the smaller area. The 6 × 2 pair has equal areas (12 = 12), and the 5 × 5 pair is bigger in both.

questions.question: A region with a larger perimeter than another region can still have a smaller area.
questions.explanation: Yes. For example a thin 9 × 1 rectangle (perimeter 20, area 9) versus a 4 × 3 rectangle (perimeter 14, area 12).

questions.question: The perimeter of a region measures which of these?
options: The product of its length and width
Half of its base times its height
The length of its boundary
The number of unit squares in it
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the length of the boundary. Counting unit squares (or length × width for a rectangle) gives area, and ½ × base × height is a triangle's area.

questions.question: Select ALL the true statements about the 7 cm × 4 cm and 8 cm × 3 cm rectangles.
options: They have the same perimeter, 22 cm
Their areas differ by 4 cm²
They have the same area, 28 cm²
The 8 × 3 rectangle has the larger area
questions.explanation: Perimeters: 2(7 + 4) = 22 and 2(8 + 3) = 22, equal. Areas: 28 and 24, so they differ by 4 cm² and the 7 × 4 rectangle is the larger.

questions.question: When the side of a square is doubled, what happens to its perimeter and its area?
options: Perimeter becomes 4 times; area doubles
Perimeter and area both become 4 times
Perimeter and area both become double
Perimeter doubles; area becomes 4 times
questions.explanation: Perimeter = 4 × side, so it doubles. Area = side × side, so doubling the side multiplies the area by 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.question: A path (shaded) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH, and the outer boundary of the path is rectangle ABCD. Which formula gives the area of the path?
options: Area(ABCD) − Area(EFGH)
Area(ABCD) + Area(EFGH)
Area(EFGH) − Area(ABCD)
Area(ABCD) ÷ Area(EFGH)
questions.explanation: The path is what remains of the outer rectangle after the park is removed, so Area(path) = Area(outer) − Area(inner).

questions.question: A park is 20 m × 10 m. A path 2 m wide runs around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
options: 200 m²
136 m²
336 m²
120 m²
questions.explanation: Outer rectangle: (20 + 4) × (10 + 4) = 24 × 14 = 336 m². Park: 200 m². Path = 336 − 200 = 136 m². 120 m² forgets the four 2 × 2 corners.

questions.question: A park is l by b, and a path of width w surrounds it on all sides. Which formula gives the area of the path?
options: (l − 2w)(b − 2w) + lb
(l + w)(b + w) − lb
(l + 2w)(b + 2w) − lb
2w(l + b)
questions.explanation: The path adds w on BOTH sides of each dimension, so the outer rectangle is (l + 2w) × (b + 2w); subtract the park lb. 2w(l + b) misses the corners.

questions.question: The outer rectangle ABCD is slid sideways while the park EFGH stays inside it (so the path is wider on one side and narrower on the other). Does the path's area change?
options: No — because the outer perimeter is unchanged
Yes — the path becomes wider on one side
Yes — the four widths are no longer equal
No — it is still outer area minus inner area
questions.explanation: The path's area is Area(ABCD) − Area(EFGH), and neither rectangle changed size. The unequal widths change the shape of the path, not its area. (Perimeter is not the reason.)

questions.question: A plot is 14 m × 12 m. Two paths, each 2 m wide, cross it — one parallel to the 14 m side and one parallel to the 12 m side. What is the area of the crosspath?
options: 48 m²
52 m²
44 m²
56 m²
questions.explanation: Path 1: 14 × 2 = 28 m². Path 2: 12 × 2 = 24 m². Their 2 × 2 = 4 m² crossing is counted twice, so area = 28 + 24 − 4 = 48 m². 52 forgets to subtract the overlap.

questions.question: For a crosspath of width w on an l × b plot, the area is lw + bw − w². Why is w² subtracted?
options: One path is shorter than the other by w
The square where the two paths cross is counted twice
The four corners of the plot are not part of the path
The paths become narrower where they meet
questions.explanation: lw and bw each include the central w × w square where the paths overlap, so it has been added twice; subtracting w² counts it once.

questions.question: Besides the plot's sides 14 m and 12 m, which measurements are needed to find the area of a crosspath?
options: The width of the path parallel to the 14 m side
The width of the path parallel to the 12 m side
The length of the diagonal of the plot
The perimeter of the plot
questions.explanation: Area of crosspath = 14 × w₁ + 12 × w₂ − w₁w₂, so only the two path widths are needed. Diagonal and perimeter play no role.

questions.question: Cutting a figure into pieces and rearranging them into a new figure never changes the total area.
questions.explanation: This is the idea behind dissection: the pieces keep their areas, so the new figure has exactly the same area as the old one.

questions.question: A diagonal is drawn in a 7 cm × 4 cm rectangle. What is the area of each of the two triangles formed?
options: 11 cm²
7 cm²
14 cm²
28 cm²
questions.explanation: The diagonal divides the rectangle into two congruent triangles, each with half the area: ½ × 7 × 4 = 14 cm².

questions.question: In two identical rectangles ABCD, point X and point Y are chosen anywhere on side AB. Which triangle has the greater area, ∆XDC or ∆YDC?
options: ∆XDC, if X is nearer to a corner
∆YDC, if Y is nearer the middle
The one whose sides are longer
Neither — each is half the rectangle
questions.explanation: Dropping the altitude from X (or Y) shows the triangle takes exactly half of each of the two smaller rectangles, so each triangle is half of ABCD regardless of where the apex is.

questions.question: In Fig. 7.1 the rectangle ABCD has sides 4 and 5 units and X lies on AB. What is the area of ∆XDC?
options: 10 sq units
9 sq units
18 sq units
20 sq units
questions.explanation: ∆XDC is half of the rectangle: ½ × 4 × 5 = 10 sq units. 20 is the whole rectangle; 9 and 18 come from adding instead of multiplying.

questions.question: ∆XDC (base DC) and ∆YBC (base BC) are drawn in two identical rectangles ABCD. Why are their areas equal even though DC ≠ BC?
options: The two triangles are congruent to each other
Each triangle is exactly half of the same rectangle
Each has perimeter equal to half the rectangle's
They have the same base and the same height
questions.explanation: Whichever side is the base, a triangle with its third vertex on the opposite side fills half the rectangle. The bases differ, so 'same base' and congruence are wrong.

questions.question: Half the area of a rectangle fills exactly half the number of its unit squares.
questions.explanation: Area is measured by counting unit squares, so halving the area halves the count of unit squares (allowing fractional squares).

questions.question: Dropping the altitude from X splits rectangle ABCD into two smaller rectangles. Which fact then proves that ∆XDC is half of ABCD?
options: The two smaller rectangles are always congruent to one another
The sides XD and XC are the two diagonals of the rectangle ABCD
XD and XC are diagonals that halve the two smaller rectangles
The altitude from X is equal in length to the base DC of the rectangle
questions.explanation: XD is a diagonal of the left rectangle and XC of the right one; each diagonal halves its rectangle, so the triangle takes half of each part, i.e. half of the whole.

questions.question: Find the area of a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides are 3 cm and 4 cm.
options: 7 cm²
5 cm²
12 cm²
6 cm²
questions.explanation: The perpendicular sides act as base and height: ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm². 12 is the full 3 × 4 rectangle; 5 is the hypotenuse length, not an area.

questions.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 5 cm and height 3.2 cm.
options: 8 cm²
4 cm²
16 cm²
8.2 cm²
questions.explanation: ½ × 5 × 3.2 = ½ × 16 = 8 cm². Forgetting the ½ gives 16; adding 5 + 3.2 gives 8.2, which is a slip.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm has the same area as a 3 cm × 4 cm rectangle.
questions.explanation: The triangle is half of that rectangle: 6 cm² versus 12 cm².

questions.question: ABCD is a rectangle with centre O (where the diagonals meet). Which of these triangles have area equal to HALF of the rectangle?
options: ∆XDC, with X anywhere on side AB
∆YBC, with Y anywhere on side AD
∆AOB, with O the centre of the rectangle
∆XMC, with M the midpoint of DC and X on AB
questions.explanation: A triangle on a full side with its apex on the opposite side is half the rectangle. ∆AOB is one of the four equal triangles made by the diagonals (a quarter), and ∆XMC uses only half of DC as base (also a quarter).

questions.question: Which formula gives the area of a triangle?
options: 2 × base × height
½ × base × height
base × height
½ × base + height
questions.explanation: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height, because the triangle is half of the rectangle built on its base and height. base × height alone is the parallelogram/rectangle formula.

questions.question: In the derivation, a line l through A parallel to BC is drawn and perpendiculars from B and C meet it at E and D. Why is the triangle's height equal to the rectangle's height?
options: AB is equal in length to side AE
BC is a diagonal of rectangle BCDE
BXAE is a rectangle, so AX = BE
A is the midpoint of the segment ED
questions.explanation: With AX ⊥ BC, the figure BXAE has four right angles, so it is a rectangle and its opposite sides AX and BE are equal — the triangle's height equals the rectangle's.

questions.question: For an obtuse triangle, the chapter writes Area(∆ABC) = ½ × h × DC − ½ × h × DB = ½ × h × BC. Which fact makes DC − DB equal to BC?
options: AD is drawn parallel to the base BC of the triangle
∆ADB and ∆ADC are congruent right triangles
D is the midpoint of the side BC of the triangle
B lies between D and C on the extended base
questions.explanation: D is the foot of the perpendicular from A on line BC extended, so B sits between D and C and DC − DB = BC. The two right triangles are not congruent and AD is perpendicular, not parallel, to BC.

questions.question: The formula ½ × base × height works only for right-angled triangles.
questions.explanation: The chapter shows it holds for all triangles — including obtuse ones, where the area is found as the difference of two right-triangle areas.

questions.question: A triangle has area 24 cm² and base 8 cm. What is its height?
options: 6 cm
3 cm
12 cm
16 cm
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height, so 24 = ½ × 8 × h = 4h, giving h = 6 cm. Using 24 ÷ 8 = 3 forgets the ½.

questions.question: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm, and the height to the 6 cm side is 4 cm. A student computes ½ × 5 × 6 = 15 cm². What went wrong?
options: The two equal sides should have been added together first
A slanted side was used instead of the perpendicular height
The ½ should not be used when the triangle is isosceles
The 6 cm side cannot be chosen as the base of the triangle
questions.explanation: Height means the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base — here 4 cm — so the area is ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². The 5 cm side is slanted, not a height.

questions.question: Which sets of measurements are enough, by themselves, to find the area of a triangle?
options: Any one side and the perpendicular height drawn to it
The sidelengths of the rectangle enclosing it on its base
Any two sides of the triangle
The perimeter of the triangle
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height needs a side and its height — which are exactly the enclosing rectangle's sidelengths. Two sides alone (without the angle) or the perimeter cannot fix the area.

questions.question: For an obtuse triangle, the area can be found as the difference of the areas of two right-angled triangles.
questions.explanation: Area(∆ABC) = Area(∆ADC) − Area(∆ADB), where D is the foot of the perpendicular from A on BC extended; both of these are right triangles.

questions.question: In ∆ABC, BC = 5, the altitude AX to BC is 3, and AC = 4. What is the length of the altitude BY drawn to AC?
options: 3.5 units
2.5 units
3.75 units
7.5 units
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × AX × BC = ½ × 3 × 5 = 7.5. Also Area = ½ × BY × AC = 2 BY. So 2 BY = 7.5 and BY = 3.75 units (7.5 is the area, not BY).

questions.question: In ∆ABC, BC = 6 units, the altitude AX to BC is 4 units and AC = 8 units. Find the altitude BY to AC.
options: 4 units
12 units
6 units
3 units
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12. With base AC: ½ × 8 × BY = 12, so 4 BY = 12 and BY = 3 units. (12 is the area, not the altitude.)

questions.question: Both diagonals of a rectangle are drawn, making four triangles. Which statement about them is correct?
options: They have equal areas but are not congruent
They have unequal areas and unequal shapes
They all have exactly the same perimeter
They are all congruent to one another in shape
questions.explanation: The chapter shows adjacent triangles have equal bases (OB = OD) and the same altitude, so all four areas are equal — though the triangles clearly have different shapes.

questions.question: Why do the adjacent triangles 1 and 2 (formed by a rectangle's diagonals) have equal areas?
options: Both are right-angled triangles with the right angle at O
Bases OB = OD and the same altitude from the common vertex
They are mirror images of each other across the diagonal
They share the side OA and the right angle at vertex O
questions.explanation: Taking OD and OB as bases, both triangles have the same altitude from the shared vertex, and OB = OD because the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other.

questions.question: A line joining a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side divides the triangle into two triangles that have…
options: congruent shapes
similar shapes
equal areas
equal perimeters
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's general statement: the two parts share the same height and have equal bases, so their areas are equal (they need not be congruent).

questions.question: ∆SUB is isosceles with SU = SB, SE is perpendicular to UB, and the area of ∆SEB is 24 sq units. What is the area of ∆SUB?
options: 24 sq units
12 sq units
96 sq units
48 sq units
questions.explanation: In an isosceles triangle the altitude to the base also bisects it, so ∆SEU and ∆SEB are congruent halves. Area(∆SUB) = 2 × 24 = 48 sq units.

questions.question: In the isosceles ∆SUB, why does the perpendicular SE split the triangle into two parts of equal area?
options: In an isosceles triangle the altitude to the base also bisects it
In every triangle an altitude bisects the opposite side
SE is exactly half as long as the base UB of the triangle
SE is parallel to the base UB, so the two halves match
questions.explanation: Only in an isosceles triangle is the altitude from the apex also the median; equal bases UE = EB and the common height SE give equal areas.

questions.question: M and N are the midpoints of XY and XZ in ∆XYZ. What fraction of the area of ∆XYZ is the area of ∆XMN?
questions.explanation: Join NY: YN is a median of ∆XYZ, so ∆XNY is half of it. Then NM is a median of ∆XNY, so ∆XMN is half of that — ½ × ½ = ¼.

questions.question: In the midpoint problem, after joining NY, why is Area(∆XNY) = ½ Area(∆XYZ)?
options: N is the centre of the triangle XYZ, so NY halves it
XN and NY are equal in length, making the triangle isosceles
NY joins vertex Y to the midpoint N of the opposite side XZ
NY is parallel to the side XM, so the heights are equal
questions.explanation: A segment from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side (a median) divides a triangle into two equal-area triangles; NY is such a median.

questions.question: In any triangle, a median always divides it into two congruent triangles.
questions.explanation: A median divides the triangle into two triangles of EQUAL AREA (same height, equal bases), but they are congruent only in special cases such as an isosceles triangle's median to the base.

questions.question: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other.
questions.explanation: This property (OB = OD) is used to show that the four triangles formed by a rectangle's diagonals have equal areas.

questions.question: Line l is parallel to BC. Triangles are drawn with base BC and third vertex anywhere on l. What can be said about their areas?
options: Largest when the apex is above the midpoint
Smallest when the apex is above the midpoint
Larger when the apex is far to one side
They are all equal
questions.explanation: All these triangles have the same base BC and the same height (the distance between the parallel lines), so ½ × base × height is the same for each.

questions.question: Among triangles with base BC and apex on a line l ∥ BC, which has the minimum perimeter?
options: The one with apex on the perpendicular bisector of BC
The one with apex above the midpoint of line l itself
They all have exactly the same perimeter length
The right-angled one with apex directly above B
questions.explanation: The reflection argument shows the shortest path B → A → C occurs when A lies on the straight line BC′, which puts A on the perpendicular bisector of BC — the isosceles triangle.

questions.question: Among triangles with base BC and apex on l ∥ BC, which has the maximum perimeter?
options: The right-angled one with apex directly above vertex C
None — sliding the apex farther along l keeps increasing it
The equilateral triangle, whenever it fits between the lines
The isosceles one with apex above the midpoint of BC
questions.explanation: Line l is endless; moving A farther and farther along it makes AB and AC as long as you like, so there is no maximum perimeter (though the area never changes).

questions.question: In the minimum-perimeter argument, why is it enough to compare only AB + AC for the different triangles?
options: BC is the longest side of every triangle
The height is the same for all the triangles
BC is a common side of all the triangles
AB and AC are always equal in length
questions.explanation: Every triangle has the same side BC, so the one with the smallest AB + AC has the smallest perimeter. Equal heights explain equal AREAS, not perimeters.

questions.question: B′ is the reflection of B in line l, and X is the foot of BB′ on l. Why is AB = AB′ for any point A on l?
options: Line l is the perpendicular bisector of segment BC
A is the midpoint of the segment BB′ on the mirror line
AB and AB′ are both parallel to the mirror line l
∆AXB ≅ ∆AXB′ (BX = B′X, right angles at X, AX common)
questions.explanation: The mirror puts B′ as far behind l as B is in front, so BX = B′X; with the right angles at X and the common side AX, the two triangles are congruent and AB = AB′.

questions.question: Which property of a plane mirror is used to locate the reflection B′ of point B?
options: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
The image distance is exactly half of the object distance
The image always appears closer to you than the object does
The image forms exactly on the reflecting surface of the mirror
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls the experimental law that the distance of the image behind the mirror equals the distance of the object in front of it.

questions.question: Using the reflection C′ of C in line l, where should A be placed on l to make B → A → C as short as possible?
options: Where the perpendicular bisector of BC′ meets l
Where the straight segment BC′ crosses line l
At the point of l that is closest to C
Where the perpendicular from B meets line l
questions.explanation: Since AC = AC′, the path B–A–C has the same length as B–A–C′, which is shortest when it is a straight line. So A is the point where BC′ cuts l.

questions.question: Gopal must walk from his house to the river and then to his water tank. Which route is shortest?
options: Walk to the river point nearest the tank, then back along the bank
Walk straight toward the tank and turn only when reaching the river
Reflect the tank in the river line; go where the house–image line meets the river
Walk to the point of the river nearest the house, then straight on to the tank
questions.explanation: This is the mirror trick: the path house → river point → tank equals house → river point → (reflected tank), which is shortest along a straight line.

questions.question: Among all triangles with base BC and apex on a line parallel to BC, the one with the least perimeter is isosceles.
questions.explanation: The reflection argument places the best apex A on the straight line BC′, which lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, so AB = AC.

questions.question: All triangles with base BC and apex on a line parallel to BC have the same perimeter.
questions.explanation: They have the same AREA (same base and height), but their perimeters differ — the isosceles one is smallest and there is no largest.

questions.question: Select the statements that are true for all triangles with base BC and apex on a line l ∥ BC.
options: They all have the same height
They all have the same area
They all have the same perimeter
They are all congruent to one another
questions.explanation: The distance between the parallel lines is the common height, so the areas are equal. Perimeters and shapes vary with the apex position.

questions.question: Why does knowing how to find the area of a triangle let us find the area of ANY polygon?
options: Every polygon is made of congruent triangles
All polygons have the same height as a triangle
A polygon's area is always three times a triangle's
Any polygon can be divided into triangles
questions.explanation: Every polygon can be cut into triangles (for example by drawing diagonals), and the polygon's area is the sum of the triangle areas.

questions.question: Joining B to D in a quadrilateral ABCD divides it into which pieces?
options: Two triangles
Two rectangles
Two trapeziums
Four triangles
questions.explanation: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into exactly two triangles, ∆ABD and ∆CBD, whose areas add up to the quadrilateral's.

questions.question: To find the area of quadrilateral ABCD by joining BD, which measurements are needed?
options: Both diagonals AC and BD of the quadrilateral ABCD
BD and the perpendicular distances of A and C from BD
BD together with the lengths of the two sides AB and CD
The lengths of all four sides of quadrilateral ABCD
questions.explanation: Each triangle needs a base and its height: BD is the common base, and the heights are the perpendiculars from A and from C to BD.

questions.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, AC = 22 cm, BM = 3 cm and DN = 3 cm, where BM and DN are perpendicular to AC. What is the area of ABCD?
options: 132 cm²
28 cm²
66 cm²
33 cm²
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 22 × 3 + ½ × 22 × 3 = 33 + 33 = 66 cm². 33 counts only one triangle; 132 forgets the halves.

questions.question: For the quadrilateral with AC = 22 cm and perpendiculars BM = DN = 3 cm, a student writes Area = ½ × 22 × 3 = 33 cm². What has been left out?
options: The second diagonal BD of the quadrilateral
The factor ½ in the triangle formula
The perimeter of the quadrilateral ABCD
The second triangle ∆ADC, with height DN
questions.explanation: The diagonal AC splits ABCD into ∆ABC (height BM) and ∆ADC (height DN). The student found only ∆ABC; adding ∆ADC gives 66 cm².

questions.question: A regular hexagon with centre O is cut by joining O to every vertex. How many triangles are formed?
questions.explanation: Joining the centre to the 6 vertices gives 6 triangles (all congruent), so the area of the hexagon is 6 times one triangle's area.

questions.question: Which construction gives a quadrilateral whose area is exactly half that of a given quadrilateral?
options: Draw one diagonal and keep one of the triangles
Join the midpoints of the four sides in order
Halve every side but keep all the angles
Join the midpoints of the two diagonals
questions.explanation: Cutting off the four corner triangles removes ¼ of each triangle made by a diagonal — ½ of the total — so the midpoint quadrilateral has half the area. Halving every side gives a quarter, and one diagonal piece is a triangle, not a quadrilateral.

questions.question: Why does joining the midpoints of a quadrilateral's sides cut its area in half?
options: The new quadrilateral is congruent to one of the two diagonal triangles
The midpoint segments are parallel to the sides, which halves the height
Each corner triangle is ¼ of the diagonal-triangle it lies in; four make ½
Each corner triangle is exactly ⅛ of the whole quadrilateral's area
questions.explanation: By the midpoint result (∆XMN = ¼ ∆XYZ), the two corners on diagonal BD remove ¼ of (∆ABD + ∆CBD) = ¼ of the whole, and likewise for diagonal AC — ½ in total.

questions.question: A quadrilateral has a diagonal of 10 cm, and the other two vertices are 4 cm and 6 cm away from it (measured perpendicularly). What is its area?
options: 100 cm²
25 cm²
240 cm²
50 cm²
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 10 × 4 + ½ × 10 × 6 = 20 + 30 = 50 cm², i.e. ½ × diagonal × (sum of the two heights).

questions.question: Whose area can be found by cutting the figure into triangles and adding them up?
options: Any quadrilateral
Any pentagon
A circle
Only regular polygons
questions.explanation: Any polygon — quadrilateral, pentagon or more — can be divided into triangles. A circle has no straight sides and cannot be cut into finitely many triangles.

questions.question: Which formula gives the area of a parallelogram?
options: base × height
base × slant side
½ × product of diagonals
½ × base × height
questions.explanation: A parallelogram can be dissected into a rectangle of the same base and height, so Area = base × height (the height is the perpendicular distance, not the slant side).

questions.question: What does the chapter call the process of cutting a figure into pieces and rearranging them into a different figure of equal area?
options: Congruence
Dissection
Tessellation
Reflection
questions.explanation: Dissection is the cut-and-rearrange process; the pieces keep their area, so the new figure has the same area as the old one.

questions.question: In the dissection of parallelogram ABCD, AX ⊥ CD is drawn, ∆AXD is cut off, and ∆BYC completes ABCX to a rectangle. Which three facts prove ∆BYC ≅ ∆AXD?
options: XC = CY, ∠BYC = ∠AXD = 90°, AB = AD
BC = AD, AB = DC, ∠BAD = ∠BCD
BY = AX, ∠BYC = ∠AXD = 90°, BC = AD
BY = AX, ∠ABY = ∠ADX, BC = AD
questions.explanation: BY = AX (opposite sides of rectangle ABYX), both have right angles, and BC = AD (opposite sides of the parallelogram) — the RHS criterion.

questions.question: Which congruence criterion is used to show ∆BYC ≅ ∆AXD in the parallelogram dissection?
options: SSS
ASA
SAS
RHS
questions.explanation: Right angle, Hypotenuse (BC = AD) and one Side (BY = AX) are matched — that is the RHS criterion for right-angled triangles.

questions.question: After the dissection, the rectangle is ABYX. Why is its base XY equal to the parallelogram's base DC?
options: DX = CY, and XC is common to both
AX and BY are both equal to DC
X and Y are the midpoints of DC
XY is a diagonal of the parallelogram
questions.explanation: DX = CY (matching sides of the congruent triangles); adding the common part XC to each gives DC = XY.

questions.question: A parallelogram has base 5 cm, a slanted side 3 cm, and height 2 cm. What is its area?
options: 30 cm²
10 cm²
15 cm²
6 cm²
questions.explanation: Area = base × height = 5 × 2 = 10 cm². Multiplying the two sides (5 × 3 = 15) is the classic mistake — the slant side is not the height.

questions.question: Parallelogram PQRS has sides 12 cm and 6 cm. The height drawn to the 6 cm side is 7.6 cm. What is the height QN drawn to the 12 cm side?
options: 4 cm
7.6 cm
3.8 cm
questions.explanation: Area = 6 × 7.6 = 45.6 cm². Using the 12 cm side as base, 12 × QN = 45.6, so QN = 3.8 cm. The longer base needs the shorter height.

questions.question: A rectangle and a parallelogram both have sidelengths 5 cm and 4 cm. Which has the greater area, and why?
options: The rectangle — because it has the larger perimeter
The parallelogram — its slanted sides make it wider
Both equal — same sides give the same base × height
The rectangle — the parallelogram's height is less than 4 cm
questions.explanation: Built on the same 5 cm base, the rectangle's height is the full 4 cm (area 20 cm²), while the parallelogram's 4 cm side leans, so its perpendicular height is less than 4 cm.

questions.question: Parallelograms (a) to (g) are drawn on the same base between the same pair of parallel lines. Which statement is correct?
options: All have equal areas; the rectangle has the least perimeter
All have equal perimeters; the rectangle has the least area
The most slanted one has the greatest area
Areas and perimeters are all equal
questions.explanation: Same base and same height ⇒ same area. Perimeters differ: the more a parallelogram leans, the longer its slanted sides, so the rectangle has the minimum perimeter.

questions.question: The area of a parallelogram can be found using any side as the base, together with the height drawn to that side.
questions.explanation: The chapter shows the parallelogram can also be cut along CZ (height to the other side) and rearranged into a rectangle, so any side and its corresponding height work.

questions.question: A parallelogram with sides 5 cm and 4 cm always has an area of 20 cm².
questions.explanation: Only the rectangle with these sides has area 20 cm². A leaning parallelogram has a height less than 4 cm, so its area is less than 20 cm².

questions.question: Select the TRUE statements about dissecting parallelogram ABCD (AX ⊥ DC) into rectangle ABYX.
options: ∆AXD is congruent to ∆BYC
Rectangle ABYX has the same height as the parallelogram
The rectangle's base XY is shorter than DC
The parallelogram's area is twice the rectangle's area
questions.explanation: The cut-off triangle fits exactly into the gap (RHS congruence) and AX is the common height. XY = DC and the areas are equal, not doubled.

questions.question: Which formula gives the area of a rhombus in terms of its diagonals?
options: diagonal × side of the rhombus
½ × product of the diagonals
product of the diagonals
½ × sum of the diagonals
questions.explanation: Dissecting a rhombus gives a rectangle of sides AC and ½ BD, so Area = ½ × AC × BD — half the product of the diagonals.

questions.question: Find the area of a rhombus whose diagonals are 20 cm and 15 cm.
options: 35 cm²
300 cm²
150 cm²
75 cm²
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 20 × 15 = 150 cm². 300 forgets the ½; 35 adds the diagonals.

questions.question: Rhombus ABCD (diagonals AC and BD) is dissected into rectangle WXYZ. What are the rectangle's sidelengths?
options: XW = AB and WZ = AD
XW = AC and WZ = BD
XW = ½ AC and WZ = ½ BD
XW = AC and WZ = ½ BD
questions.explanation: The two isosceles triangles ∆ABD and ∆CBD each become a rectangle of width ½ BD; joined along their heights they form a rectangle AC long and ½ BD wide.

questions.question: Adding Area(∆ADB) = ½ × AO × BD and Area(∆CDB) = ½ × CO × BD gives ½ × BD × (AO + CO). Which fact turns AO + CO into AC?
options: O lies on AC, because the diagonals cut each other
AO and CO are each equal to half of the diagonal BD
O is the midpoint of the diagonal BD, not of AC
AO is perpendicular to CO, meeting at the point O
questions.explanation: O is the intersection of the diagonals, so it lies on AC and AO + CO = AC. This gives ½ × BD × AC, the same formula as before.

questions.question: How can a rectangle of length l and width w be converted into a rhombus of equal area by dissection?
options: Make a rhombus with diagonals l and w
Make a rhombus with diagonals l and 2w
Make a rhombus with diagonals 2l and 2w
Make a rhombus with sides l and w
questions.explanation: Reverse the rhombus dissection: a rhombus with diagonals l and 2w has area ½ × l × 2w = lw, exactly the rectangle's area.

questions.question: A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm. Using base × height, what is its height?
options: 8.0 cm
6.4 cm
9.6 cm
4.8 cm
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 16 × 12 = 96 cm². Half-diagonals 8 and 6 give side = √(8² + 6²) = 10 cm. So height = 96 ÷ 10 = 9.6 cm.

questions.question: Since a rhombus is a parallelogram, base × height also gives its area.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the parallelogram formula holds for a rhombus; the diagonal formula is an additional method.

questions.question: The area of a rhombus equals the product of its two diagonals.
questions.explanation: It is HALF the product of the diagonals — the dissection rectangle has sides AC and ½ BD.

questions.question: A square is a rhombus. If a square has diagonals of 10 cm, what is its area?
options: 100 cm²
25 cm²
20 cm²
50 cm²
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². (100 would need the side, not the diagonal, to be 10 cm.)

questions.question: Which properties of a rhombus are used in dissecting it into a rectangle?
options: Its diagonals are perpendicular to each other
Its diagonals bisect each other
Its diagonals are equal in length
All its angles are right angles
questions.explanation: Perpendicular, bisecting diagonals make ∆ABD and ∆CBD isosceles with the half-diagonals as heights. Equal diagonals and right angles belong to a square, not every rhombus.

questions.question: Which formula gives the area of a trapezium?
options: ½ × height × sum of the parallel sides
½ × height × difference of the parallel sides
½ × product of the parallel sides
height × sum of the parallel sides
questions.explanation: Area of a trapezium = ½ × h × (a + b), where a and b are the parallel sides and h the perpendicular distance between them.

questions.question: A trapezium has parallel sides 24 m and 36 m and height 14 m. What is its area?
options: 210 m²
420 m²
336 m²
840 m²
questions.explanation: ½ × 14 × (24 + 36) = 7 × 60 = 420 m². 840 forgets the ½; 336 is 24 × 14 (a rectangle).

questions.question: In trapezium WXYZ (WX ∥ ZY), WM and XN are drawn perpendicular to ZY. Why is WXNM a rectangle?
options: WX = MN because WM and XN are both diagonals of the figure
The base angles at Z and Y are equal, which makes WXNM a square
∠MWX = ∠NXW = 90°, as co-interior angles with WX ∥ ZY sum to 180°
WM and XN are equal because W and X are midpoints of the top side
questions.explanation: WM is a transversal of the parallels WX and ZY; the interior angles on the same side add to 180°, and one is 90°, so the other is 90° too. Same for XN.

questions.question: In the derivation the area ½h(x + y + 2a) becomes ½h(a + b) using x + y = b − a. Which length is b?
options: The slanted side WZ of the trapezium
The height of the trapezium (= WM)
The shorter parallel side WX (= a)
The longer parallel side ZY (= x + a + y)
questions.explanation: ZY is made of MZ = x, MN = a and NY = y, so b = x + y + a and x + y = b − a. Substituting gives ½h(a + b).

questions.question: Two copies of a trapezium (AB ∥ CD) are joined along BC, the second one rotated. Why is the result a quadrilateral and not a 6-sided figure?
options: x + y = 180° (co-interior angles), so ABD′ and A′CD are straight lines
x = y, because the two copies of the trapezium are congruent
The rotation turns all four angles of the figure into 90°
BC becomes a diagonal, and a diagonal always gives four sides
questions.explanation: Angles x and y are interior angles on the same side of transversal BC between the parallels AB and CD, so they add to 180° and the sides line up into straight lines.

questions.question: The two joined copies form a parallelogram. What are its base and height, if the trapezium has parallel sides a, b and height h?
options: Base b − a, height h
Base a + b, height h
Base a + b, height 2h
Base ½(a + b), height h
questions.explanation: The parallelogram has base a + b and the same height h, area h(a + b); the trapezium is half of it: ½h(a + b).

questions.question: A regular hexagon is divided into a trapezium, an equilateral triangle and a rhombus. What is the ratio of their areas?
questions.explanation: A regular hexagon is 6 equal equilateral triangles. The trapezium is half the hexagon (3 triangles), the rhombus is 2 triangles and the equilateral triangle is 1 — ratio 3 : 1 : 2.

questions.question: ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY, and ZA extended meets WX extended at B. Why is Area(ZYXW) = Area(∆ZWB)?
options: The trapezium and triangle share the same height and base
ZA is a median of ∆ZWB, so it halves the triangle
ZY = XB, because A is the midpoint of ZB
∆ZYA ≅ ∆BXA, so the cut-off piece exactly refills the gap
questions.explanation: A is the midpoint of XY, the vertical angles at A are equal and ZY ∥ WB gives equal alternate angles, so ∆ZYA ≅ ∆BXA (ASA). Swapping these equal pieces turns the trapezium into ∆ZWB.

questions.question: Trapezium ABCD is converted into rectangle EFGH by cutting along the perpendiculars through the midpoints I and J of its legs. The rectangle's height equals the trapezium's; what is its width?
options: Half the sum of the parallel sides
The sum of the parallel sides
The longer parallel side
Half the difference of the parallel sides
questions.explanation: Equal areas with the same height h means width × h = ½h(a + b), so the width is ½(a + b) — the segment IJ joining the midpoints of the legs.

questions.question: Which trapezium has an area of 144 cm²?
options: Height 6 cm, parallel sides 20 cm and 24 cm
Height 12 cm, parallel sides 10 cm and 14 cm
Height 12 cm, parallel sides 12 cm and 24 cm
Height 8 cm, parallel sides 8 cm and 10 cm
questions.explanation: ½ × 12 × (10 + 14) = 144 cm². The others give 216, 72 and 132 cm².

questions.question: The formula ½ × height × (sum of parallel sides) holds only for isosceles trapeziums.
questions.explanation: The chapter derives it for a general trapezium (and shows two approaches even for the slanted-over kind); it holds for every trapezium.

questions.question: Approach 2 for a slanted trapezium — drawing BG parallel to AD — splits the trapezium into a parallelogram and a triangle.
questions.explanation: ABGD becomes a parallelogram (AB ∥ DG and BG ∥ AD) and the remaining piece ∆BGC is a triangle.

questions.question: Two copies of a trapezium (parallel sides a, b; height h) are joined along a leg. Select the TRUE statements.
options: The combined figure is a parallelogram
The combined figure has base a + b
The combined figure has height 2h
The combined area is half the trapezium's area
questions.explanation: The figure is a parallelogram of base a + b and height h (not 2h) and area h(a + b) — twice the trapezium's area.

questions.question: What are the Śulba-Sūtras?
options: Ancient Greek texts on the properties of circles
Medieval Indian tables used for astronomy
Ancient Indian geometric texts on constructing altars
Ancient Chinese manuals for surveying farmland
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the Śulba-Sūtras as ancient Indian geometric texts dealing with the construction of altars, which contain many problems on areas.

questions.question: Why did the Śulba-Sūtras contain problems about transforming one shape into another of the same area?
options: Land had to be divided fairly among farmers
Builders wanted to use the least possible bricks
Scribes needed to copy drawings onto smaller pages
Altars had to have an exactly prescribed shape and area
questions.explanation: When altars were built they had to have the exact prescribed shape and area, so one often needed to change a given shape into a different one of equal area.

questions.question: Besides the Śulba-Sūtras, in which famous text does the chapter say such equal-area problems are also posed and solved?
options: Euclid's Elements
Āryabhaṭa's Āryabhaṭīya
Bhāskara's Līlāvatī
Archimedes' Sand Reckoner
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that problems of transforming a shape into another of equal area are also found in Euclid's Elements.

questions.question: A rectangle has length l and width w. Which triangle has the same area as the rectangle?
options: Base l and height w
Base l and height 2w
Base 2l and height 2w
Base ½l and height w
questions.explanation: Triangle area ½ × l × 2w = lw. With height w the triangle would be only half the rectangle; with 2l and 2w it would be double.

questions.question: A triangle has base b and height h. Which rectangle has the same area as the triangle?
options: Base b and width h
Base ½b and width ½h
Base b and width ½h
Base 2b and width h
questions.explanation: Rectangle area b × ½h = ½bh. (Cut the triangle along the line halfway up and rearrange the top piece.) Base b with width h gives double the area.

questions.question: An isosceles triangle ABC (AB = AC) has altitude AD. ∆ADB and ∆ADC are rearranged into a rectangle. What are the rectangle's sides?
options: AD and BC (the full base)
AB and AC (the equal sides)
AB and BD (half the base)
AD and BD (half the base)
questions.explanation: The two congruent right triangles each form half of a rectangle with legs AD and BD; placed together they make one AD × BD rectangle, area ½ × BC × AD, the same as the triangle.

questions.question: Which has the greater area: two identical equilateral triangles of side s placed together, or a square of side s?
options: The square, because the triangles' total is s × h with h < s
The two triangles, because together they have six sides
They are exactly equal, because 2 × ½ × s × s equals s × s
The two triangles, because their height is more than s
questions.explanation: Two triangles give 2 × ½ × s × h = s × h, where the height h of an equilateral triangle is less than its side s. So s × h < s × s, the square's area.

questions.question: How can an isosceles trapezium be converted into a rectangle by dissection?
options: Cut off both end triangles and simply throw them away
Cut off one end triangle and fit it, flipped, against the other end
Cut along the midline and stack the two halves together
Cut along one diagonal and swap the two triangles over
questions.explanation: Dropping perpendiculars from the top vertices leaves a middle rectangle and two congruent right triangles; one triangle flipped onto the other makes a second rectangle, giving one rectangle in total.

questions.question: The Śulba-Sūtras give methods to change one shape into another of equal area.
questions.explanation: Altar construction required exact areas, so the Śulba-Sūtras solve problems such as turning a rectangle into a triangle (or rhombus, or isosceles triangle) of the same area.

questions.question: A rectangle and a triangle with the same base and the same height have equal areas.
questions.explanation: The triangle has HALF the rectangle's area. To match areas the triangle needs double the height (or the rectangle half the width).

questions.question: To convert a rectangle into an isosceles triangle of equal area by dissection, the triangle should have…
options: base and height both twice the rectangle's sides
base half of one side and height equal to the other
base twice one side and height equal to the other side
base equal to one side and height equal to the other
questions.explanation: Reverse the isosceles-triangle dissection: a rectangle AD × BD becomes a triangle with base 2 × BD and height AD, area ½ × 2BD × AD = AD × BD.

questions.question: An A4 sheet has sidelengths 21 cm and 29.7 cm. What is its area?
options: 6237 cm²
questions.explanation: 21 × 29.7 = 623.7 cm². (101.4 is the perimeter in cm; the other two have the decimal point misplaced.)

questions.question: Given 1 in = 2.54 cm, express 5 in in centimetres.
options: 127 cm
questions.explanation: 5 × 2.54 = 12.7 cm. Adding (5 + 2.54) or dividing (5 ÷ 2.54 ≈ 1.97) are the common slips.

questions.question: Express 11.43 cm in inches (1 in = 2.54 cm).
options: 5.5 in
4.5 in
questions.explanation: 11.43 ÷ 2.54 = 4.5 in (since 4 × 2.54 = 10.16 and 0.5 × 2.54 = 1.27). Multiplying instead gives 29.03.

questions.question: How many cm² make 1 in²?
options: 5.08 cm²
2.54 cm²
questions.explanation: A square inch is 2.54 cm by 2.54 cm, so 1 in² = 2.54² = 6.4516 cm². (64.516 cm² is 10 in².)

questions.question: Convert 10 in² to cm².
options: 25.4 cm²
questions.explanation: 10 × 6.4516 = 64.516 cm². Using 2.54 instead of 2.54² gives the wrong 25.4.

questions.question: Convert 161.29 cm² to in².
options: 25 in²
2.5 in²
63.5 in²
questions.explanation: Every 6.4516 cm² is one in², so 161.29 ÷ 6.4516 = 25 in². Dividing by 2.54 (giving 63.5) is the trap — area needs the squared factor.

questions.question: How many in² are there in 1 ft²? (1 ft = 12 in)
options: 144 in²
12 in²
24 in²
questions.explanation: 1 ft² = 12 in × 12 in = 144 in². 12 forgets to square; 1,728 is 12³.

questions.question: How many square feet make 1 acre?
questions.explanation: The chapter states 1 acre = 43,560 ft². Acres are used for larger areas of land.

questions.question: How many m² are there in 1 km²?
questions.explanation: 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 km² = 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 m² (10⁶). Squaring 1000 wrongly as 10⁷ or 10⁵ gives the other values.

questions.question: Which of these are local units of AREA used in parts of India, as listed in the chapter?
options: bigha
cent
kilogram
furlong
litre
questions.explanation: The chapter lists bigha, gaj, katha, dhur, cent and ankanam as local area units. A kilogram measures mass, a furlong length and a litre volume.

questions.question: Why is 1 in² equal to 2.54² cm² rather than 2.54 cm²?
options: Both length and width of the square convert, so 2.54 is used twice
The factor is squared only when the area is bigger than 1 in²
An inch is officially defined as 2.54² centimetres in length
Square units are always exactly 2 times the length units
questions.explanation: A square inch is 2.54 cm long AND 2.54 cm wide, so its area is 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 cm² — the conversion factor appears once for each dimension.

questions.question: 1 ft² equals 12 in².
questions.explanation: 1 ft² = 12 in × 12 in = 144 in², because both sides of the square foot are 12 inches.

questions.question: Larger areas of land are measured in acres, and 1 acre = 43,560 ft².
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the chapter; even larger areas (towns, cities) are measured in km².
